[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Afro-Eurasia_%28orthographic_projection%29_political.svg/250px-Afro-Eurasia_%28orthographic_projection%29_political.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Afro-Eurasia_(orthographic_projection)_political.svg)

Afro-Eurasia

Geographical Asia is a cultural artifact of European conceptions of the world, beginning with the [Ancient Greeks](/wiki/Ancient_Greeks "Ancient Greeks"), being imposed onto other cultures, an imprecise concept causing endemic contention about what it means. Asia does not exactly correspond to the cultural borders of its various types of constituents.[[48]](#cite_note-50)

From the time of Herodotus, a minority of geographers have rejected the three-continent system (Europe, Africa, Asia) on the grounds that there is no substantial physical separation between them.[[49]](#cite_note-51) For example, Sir [Barry Cunliffe](/wiki/Barry_Cunliffe "Barry Cunliffe"), the emeritus professor of European archeology at Oxford, argues that Europe has been geographically and culturally merely "the western excrescence of the continent of Asia".[[50]](#cite_note-52)

Geographically, Asia is the major eastern constituent of the continent of [Eurasia](/wiki/Eurasia "Eurasia") with Europe being a northwestern [peninsula](/wiki/Peninsula "Peninsula") of the landmass. Asia, Europe and Africa make up a single continuous landmass—[Afro-Eurasia](/wiki/Afro-Eurasia "Afro-Eurasia")—and share a common [continental shelf](/wiki/Continental_shelf "Continental shelf"). Almost all of Europe and a major part of Asia sit atop the [Eurasian Plate](/wiki/Eurasian_Plate "Eurasian Plate"), adjoined on the south by the [Arabian](/wiki/Arabian_Plate "Arabian Plate") and [Indian Plate](/wiki/Indian_Plate "Indian Plate") and with the easternmost part of Siberia (east of the [Chersky Range](/wiki/Chersky_Range "Chersky Range")) on the [North American Plate](/wiki/North_American_Plate "North Ameri

Aquatic biodiversity in the Mekong River system is the second highest in the world after the [Amazon](/wiki/Amazon_River "Amazon River").[[50]](#cite_note-ICEM2010-51)[[51]](#cite_note-Fergusonetal2011-52)
The Mekong boasts the most concentrated [biodiversity](/wiki/Biodiversity "Biodiversity") per hectare of any river.[[52]](#cite_note-VJetal2009-53) The largest recorded freshwater fish, a 300 kg (660 lb) [giant freshwater stingray](/wiki/Giant_freshwater_stingray "Giant freshwater stingray") in 2022 and previously a 293 kg (646 lb) [Mekong giant catfish](/wiki/Mekong_giant_catfish "Mekong giant catfish") in 2005, were both caught in the Mekong River.[[53]](#cite_note-54)

The commercially valuable fish species in the Mekong are generally divided between "black fish", which inhabit low oxygen, slow moving, shallow waters, and "white fish", which inhabit well oxygenated, fast moving, deeper waters.[[54]](#cite_note-MRC_2010b-55) People living within the Mekong River system generate many other sources of food and income from what are often termed "other aquatic animals" (OAAs) such as freshwater crabs, shrimp, snakes, turtles, and frogs.

OAAs account for about 20% of the total Mekong catch.[[4]](#cite_note-MRC_2010a-5) When fisheries are discussed, catches are typically divided between the wild capture fishery (i.e., fish and other aquatic animals caught in their natural habitat), and aquaculture (fish reared under controlled conditions). **South Korea**,[[b]](#cite_note-11) officially the **Republic of Korea** (**ROK**),[[c]](#cite_note-12) is a country in [East Asia](/wiki/East_Asia "East Asia"). It constitutes the southern half of the [Korean Peninsula](/wiki/Korea "Korea") and borders [North Korea](/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea") along the [Korean Demilitarized Zone](/wiki/Korean_Demilitarized_Zone "Korean Demilitarized Zone"), with the [Yellow Sea](/wiki/Yellow_Sea "Yellow Sea") to the west and the [Sea of Japan](/wiki/Sea_of_Japan "Sea of Japan") to the east. South Korea claims to be the sole legitimate government of the entire peninsula and [adjacent islands](/wiki/List_of_islands_of_South_Korea "List of islands of South Korea"). It has [a population](/wiki/Demographics_of_South_Korea "Demographics of South Korea") of about 52 million, of which half live in the [Seoul metropolitan area](/wiki/Seoul_metropolitan_area "Seoul metropolitan area"), the [ninth most populous metropolitan area in the world](/wiki/List_of_largest_cities "List of largest cities"), with other major cities being [Busan](/wiki/Busan "Busan"), [Daegu](/wiki/Daegu "Daegu"), and [Incheon](/wiki/Incheon "Incheon").

The Korean Peninsula was inhabited as early as the [Lower Paleolithic](/wiki/Lower_Paleolithic "Lower Paleolithic") period. [Its first kingdom](/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn "Old Chosŏn") was noted in Chinese records in the early seventh century BC. From the mid first century BC,[[10]](#cite_note-13) various [polities](/wiki/Polity "Polity") consolidated into the rival [kingdoms](/wiki/Three_Kingdoms_of_Korea "Three Kingdoms of Korea") of [Goguryeo](/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo"), [Baekje](/wiki/Baekje "Baekje"), and [Silla](/wiki/Silla "Silla"). The lattermost eventually [unified most of the peninsula](/wiki/Unified_Silla "Unified Silla") for the first time in the late seventh century AD, while [Balhae](/wiki/Balhae "Balhae") succeeded Goguryeo in the north. fanoutqa_033863.t: 2018 California wildfires :: Causes :: Increase in fuel :: chunk_0003
fanoutqa_033863.x:
2018 California wildfires :: Causes :: Increase in fuel :: chunk_0003
A direct contributor to the 2018 California wildfires was an increase in dead tree fuel.[[35]](#cite_note-35) By December 2017, there were a record 129 million dead trees in California.[[36]](#cite_note-36) Tree mortality is linked to a period during the 2010s of "anomalously warm droughts" [[37]](#cite_note-:1-37) that were severe and long-lasting enough to stand out even amongst California's existing history of wildfires and [exceptionally dry conditions](/wiki/Droughts_in_California "Droughts in California").[[34]](#cite_note-:03-34) One study focused on the concentrated mortality of densely populated conifers of the Sierra Nevada "found that die-off was closely tied to multi-year deep-rooting-zone drying" and that severity of that dryness can be used to predict mortality.[[37]](#cite_note-:1-37) Such drought leaves trees stressed for water, which makes them susceptible to beetle infestation and exacerbates tree mortality further.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

Drought intensity lessened in California by 2017,[[39]](#cite_note-39) but the effects of tree mortality linger for years. One study expresses a lack of sufficient data to confidently determine the rate of coniferous tree decay in the Sierra Nevada.[[40]](#cite_note-40) Nonetheless, it is a gradual process, and the remaining dead tree matter is an optimal fuel source for future wild fires.

fanoutqa_017991.x:
History of the Internet :: Foundations :: Precursors :: Computers and modems :: chunk_0003
:   Early fixed-program [computers](/wiki/Computer "Computer") in the 1940s were operated manually by entering small programs via [switches](/wiki/Switch "Switch") in order to load and run a series of programs. As [transistor](/wiki/Transistor "Transistor") technology evolved in the 1950s, [central processing units](/wiki/Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") and user [terminals](/wiki/Computer_terminal "Computer terminal") came into use by 1955. The [mainframe computer](/wiki/Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer") model was devised, and [modems](/wiki/Modem "Modem"), such as the [Bell 101](/wiki/Bell_101_modem "Bell 101 modem"), allowed [digital data](/wiki/Digital_data "Digital data") to be transmitted over regular unconditioned [telephone lines](/wiki/Telephone_line "Telephone line") at low speeds by the late 1950s. These technologies made it possible to exchange data between [remote computers](/wiki/Remote_desktop_software "Remote desktop software"). However, a fixed-line link was still necessary; the point-to-point communication model did not allow for direct communication between any two arbitrary systems. In addition, the applications were specific and not general purpose. Examples included [SAGE](/wiki/Semi-Automatic_Ground_Environment "Semi-Automatic Ground Environment") (1958) and [SABRE](/wiki/Sabre_(travel_reservation_system) "Sabre (travel reservation system)") (1960).

Wilkins notched his first [Slam-Dunk Championship](/wiki/NBA_Slam_Dunk_Contest "NBA Slam Dunk Contest") at the [NBA All-Star Weekend](/wiki/NBA_All-Star_Weekend "NBA All-Star Weekend") in Indianapolis during the 1984–85 season. He went on to finish the season with a 27.4 scoring average, good for sixth in the NBA. He ranked second on the Hawks in rebounding (6.9 rpg) and steals (135). For the first of two straight seasons, he led the NBA in field-goal attempts, with 1,891. After going 0-for-11 from the three-point line the previous season, Wilkins made 25 of 81 three-point shots in 1984–85. He also shot better than 80 percent from the free throw line for the first of 10 consecutive seasons. Despite Wilkins's efforts, Atlanta finished 34–48 and failed to reach the playoffs.

Wilkins exploded into the NBA's elite circle in 1985–86, winning the league scoring title with an average of 30.3 points per game. He was an [NBA All-Star](/wiki/NBA_All-Star "NBA All-Star") for the first time and was voted to the [All-NBA](/wiki/All-NBA "All-NBA") First Team at the end of the season. He failed in his bid to repeat as NBA Slam-Dunk champion, his competition coming from an unlikely source. The Hawks had signed 5-foot-7 [Anthony "Spud" Webb](/wiki/Spud_Webb "Spud Webb") as a free agent prior to the season, and Webb dazzled the All-Star Saturday crowd in Dallas by soaring more than 4 feet (1.2 m) to the basket on each of his dunk attempts. Atlanta turned its fortunes around in dramatic fashion, winning 16 more games in the 1985–86 season to finish 50–32 for the year. Wilkins scored 57 points in one game and ranked among the Hawks' leaders in rebounding (7.9 rpg), steals (138), and free-throw percentage (.818). The [Americas](/wiki/Americas "Americas") were named after the [Italian](/wiki/Italians "Italians") explorer [Amerigo Vespucci](/wiki/Amerigo_Vespucci "Amerigo Vespucci") by [German](/wiki/German_people "German people") cartographers [Martin Waldseemüller](/wiki/Martin_Waldseem%C3%BCller "Martin Waldseemüller") and [Matthias Ringmann](/wiki/Matthias_Ringmann "Matthias Ringmann").[[15]](#cite_note-18) Vespucci explored [South America](/wiki/South_America "South America") between 1497 and 1502, and was the first European to suggest that the Americas represented a landmass then unknown to the Europeans. In 1507, Waldseemüller published a world map, and placed the word "America" on the continent of present-day South America.[[16]](#cite_note-19) The continent north of present-day Mexico was then referred to as Parias.[[17]](#cite_note-20) On a 1553 world map published by [Petrus Apianus](/wiki/Petrus_Apianus "Petrus Apianus"),[[18]](#cite_note-21) North America was called "Baccalearum", meaning "realm of the Cod fish", in reference to the abundance of [cod](/wiki/Cod "Cod") on the [East Coast](/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United

Head office of [Industrial and Commercial Bank of China](/wiki/Industrial_and_Commercial_Bank_of_China "Industrial and Commercial Bank of China"), the world’s largest bank by total assets

This list is based on the April 2025 [S&P Global Market Intelligence](/wiki/S%26P_Global_Market_Intelligence "S&P Global Market Intelligence") report of the 100 largest banks in the world. The ranking was based upon assets as reported and was not adjusted for different accounting treatments.[[1]](#cite_note-SP-1) Another publication which compiles an annual list of the world's largest banks is *[The Banker](/wiki/The_Banker "The Banker")* magazine. It publishes a list of the World 1000 Largest Banks every July.[[2]](#cite_note-2) The financial data published by the July yearly issue of *The Banker* are much more extensive compared to the S&P Top 100 banks, but it is not a publication intended for the general public.

Accounting treatment affects the assets reported: for example, the United States uses [US GAAP](/wiki/Generally_Accepted_Accounting_Principles_(United_States) "Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (United States)") (as opposed to [IFRS](/wiki/International_Financial_Reporting_Standards "International Financial Reporting Standards")), which only reports the net [derivative](/wiki/Derivative_(finance) "Derivative (finance)") position in most cases, leading to US banks having fewer derivative assets than comparable non-US banks.[[3]](#cite_note-3) When adjusted forward this netting, JPMorgan Chase would have US$4,607.43 billion in total assets, rather than US$4,002.81 billion.[[1]](#cite_note-SP-1) However, this has no impact on the ranking of the bank.
